questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
questions.worked_solution:
We use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡x+{sin}^{2}⁡x=1
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }(14{cos}^{2}⁡x-5{x}^{2}+14{sin}^{2}⁡x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(14({sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(14\cdot 1-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }(14-5{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =(14x-\frac{5}{3}{x}^{3})\,{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =[14\pi -\frac{5}{3}{\pi }^{3}]-[14\cdot 0-\frac{5}{3}\cdot {0}^{3}] \\  & =14\pi -\frac{5{\pi }^{3}}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,{cos}^{2}⁡x=1-{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x})\text{d}x \\  & =\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+\operatorname{sec}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,1-{sin}^{2}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{2\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /3} \\  & =2[\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(0)] \\  & =2(2-1) \\  & =2\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-{sec}^{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we select the identity that contains a $\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x-1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x-{sec}^{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{(-\operatorname{sec}⁡x)({sec}^{2}⁡x-1)}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x{tan}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3}\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\operatorname{sec}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /4}^{\pi /3} \\  & =-[\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sec}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})] \\  & =-[2-\sqrt{2}] \\  & =\sqrt{2}-2\end{aligned}
$$

First, we select the identity that contains a ${tan}^{2}⁡x$ term. We can use the identity 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡x={sec}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\frac{9-9{tan}^{4}⁡x}{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =9{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\frac{1-{tan}^{4}⁡x}{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =9{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}\frac{(1-{tan}^{2}⁡x)(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)}{1-{tan}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =9{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}(1+{tan}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =9{\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6}{sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =9\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,{|}_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /6} \\  & =9\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6})-9\operatorname{tan}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =9\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}-9(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}) \\  & =3\sqrt{3}+3\sqrt{3} \\  & =6\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have to use the identity

$$
1+{cot}^{2}⁡x={csc}^{2}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{{cot}^{2}⁡x-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1-{cot}^{4}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{{cot}^{2}⁡x-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1-{cot}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1-{cot}^{2}⁡x)(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x(1+{cot}^{2}⁡x)}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x{csc}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{\int }_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,{|}_{\pi /3}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =0-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int (9{tan}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )-5{x}^{4}+9)\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the identity  $1+{tan}^{2}⁡\theta ={sec}^{2}⁡\theta $ with $\theta =(5x+\pi ),$ we get 

$$
1+{tan}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )={sec}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi ).
$$

Substituting the above into our integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (9{tan}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )-5{x}^{4}+9)\,\text{d}x & =\int (9[1+{tan}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )]-5{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int (9{sec}^{2}⁡(5x+\pi )-5{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & =9\cdot (\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡(5x+\pi ))-5\cdot \frac{{x}^{5}}{5}+C \\  & =\frac{9}{5}\operatorname{tan}⁡(5x+\pi )-{x}^{5}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use a variation of the Pythagorean identity:

$$
\sin^2 x + \cos^2 x = 1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad  \cos^2 x = 1-\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the above, we rewrite the denominator and calculate the resulting integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {(\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x})}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we select the identity that contains a $\tan^2{x}$ term. So we can use the identity 

$$
1+\tan^2x =\sec^2x.
$$

Rearranging the above identity gives

$$
\tan^2 x =\sec^2 x -1.
$$

Using the above, we compute the given integral as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \tan^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \left(\sec^2 x -1\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\tan x -x+C.	
	}
$$

In this case, we have to use the identity  $1+\cot^2x =\csc^2 x.$ Rearranging this gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\cot^2 x &=\csc^2 x -1.
}
$$

Substituting this into our integral gives

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \left(5\cot^2 x -x^2\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \bigg(5\left(\csc^2 x -1 \right) -x^2\bigg) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=\int \left(5\csc^2 x -5 -x^2\right ) \, \textrm{d}x\
				&=-5\cot x -5x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}+C.	
	}
$$

		\int 2\tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x&= 2\int \tan^2 (3x) \, \textrm{d}x\
